title: How to Create a Scope of Work for a House Flip (Step-by-Step Guide)
excerpt: A solid scope of work can make or break your house flip — it keeps contractors accountable, protects your budget, and helps you close on time. Learn exactly how to build one from scratch with real examples and numbers.
author: AIWholesail Team

metaDescription: Learn how to create a scope of work for a house flip with step-by-step guidance, real examples, and cost breakdowns to protect your budget and maximize profit.

sections.content: One of the most expensive mistakes a house flipper can make is handing a contractor a key and saying "fix it up." Without a detailed scope of work, you are inviting budget overruns, missed deadlines, and disagreements that can eat your entire profit margin. If you want to flip houses successfully, learning how to create a scope of work for a house flip is non-negotiable. This guide walks you through every step, from your first walkthrough to the final signed document. If you are still learning the fundamentals of evaluating deals before you get to the rehab phase, start with our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-deal-analysis).
What Is a Scope of Work?

A scope of work (SOW) is a written document that describes every single repair, renovation, and improvement you plan to make on a property. It tells contractors exactly what needs to be done, which materials to use, what quality standards are expected, and often includes a line-item budget for each task. Think of it as the blueprint for your entire rehab project. A strong SOW protects you legally, helps you get accurate bids from multiple contractors, and keeps the project on schedule from day one.
Why a Scope of Work Is Critical for Profitability

Flipping a house is a business, and your SOW is your business plan for that property. Without it, contractors have no clear reference point, which leads to change orders — and change orders cost money. According to industry data, renovation projects without a detailed scope go over budget by 20% to 40% on average. On a $50,000 rehab budget, that is a $10,000 to $20,000 surprise. Your SOW also directly affects your [Maximum Allowable Offer (MAO)](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/maximum-allowable-offer-formula), because you cannot calculate what you can safely pay for a property without knowing your total rehab costs first.
Step 1 — Walk the Property Room by Room

Before you write a single word, you need to physically walk every inch of the property with a notepad or voice recorder. Go room by room and document every defect, every system that needs updating, and every cosmetic issue you see. Do not skip the attic, crawl space, or basement. Check the roof from outside, run every faucet, flip every switch, and test every outlet. Take photos of everything. This walkthrough is the foundation of your entire scope of work, and what you miss here will come back to haunt you during construction.

Pro Tip: Bring a flashlight, a plug-in outlet tester (available at any hardware store for under $10), and a moisture meter on your walkthrough. Catching hidden water damage or electrical issues before you write your SOW can save you thousands in unexpected repair costs.
Step 2 — Organize Your Findings by Category

Once you have your notes, organize everything into standard renovation categories. This makes it easy to assign tasks to the right subcontractors and get clean, apples-to-apples bids. Most experienced flippers use categories like these:

items: Structural — foundation repairs, load-bearing walls, framing issues
Roof and Exterior — shingles, gutters, siding, paint, driveway, landscaping
Plumbing — pipe repairs, water heater replacement, fixture upgrades
Electrical — panel upgrades, wiring, outlets, light fixtures
HVAC — furnace, AC unit, ductwork, thermostats
Insulation and Drywall — damaged drywall, insulation gaps, ceiling repairs
Flooring — hardwood refinishing, new LVP, tile, carpet
Kitchen — cabinets, countertops, appliances, backsplash, sink
Bathrooms — vanities, toilets, tile, tub/shower, mirrors
Doors and Windows — replacements, hardware, weatherstripping
Paint — interior and exterior, color selections
Cleaning and Haul-Off — junk removal, final clean

sections.content: Step 3 — Write Line-Item Descriptions for Each Task

This is where most beginners fall short. Vague descriptions lead to vague bids. Instead of writing "update kitchen," write "remove and replace existing laminate countertops with 30 linear feet of 3cm granite in a color approved by owner; install new undermount stainless steel single-basin sink and chrome faucet." The more specific you are, the harder it is for a contractor to misinterpret the job or substitute cheaper materials without your knowledge. Include brand names, product lines, dimensions, and finish levels wherever possible.
Example Line Item: Flooring

Here is a real-world example of a detailed flooring line item: "Remove existing carpet and padding in all three bedrooms (approx. 480 sq ft total). Install Shaw Floorte Pro 5-Series LVP in 'Mineral' colorway, 6mm thickness with attached pad. Include all transition strips and quarter-round trim. Dispose of all old material off-site." This level of detail means every contractor bidding the job is pricing the same exact work, so your comparisons are meaningful.
Step 4 — Assign Budget Numbers to Each Line Item

After you have described every task, attach a budgeted cost to each line. These numbers come from contractor bids, past project data, or reliable cost estimating tools. Our free [Rehab Estimator at aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator) can help you build realistic cost ranges by trade and market so you are not guessing. For example, a full kitchen remodel on a mid-range flip in a market like [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) might run $12,000 to $18,000, while the same work in [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) or [Las Vegas, NV](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/las-vegas-nv) could look different based on local labor rates. Always get at least three contractor bids and compare them to your internal estimates.

"The budget you set before construction is the profit you protect after the sale. Every dollar of scope creep comes straight out of your check at closing." — Experienced house flipper and real estate investor
Step 5 — Include a Contingency Reserve

Even the best scope of work will encounter surprises — hidden mold behind drywall, outdated plumbing behind the walls, or a roof deck that needs full replacement instead of just new shingles. Standard practice is to add a 10% to 15% contingency reserve to your total rehab budget. On a $60,000 renovation, that means setting aside $6,000 to $9,000 for the unexpected. This contingency is not a line item you spend freely — it is an emergency fund for legitimate surprises only. Also remember to factor in [holding costs](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/holding-costs-real-estate) like loan interest, property taxes, insurance, and utilities, which accumulate every day the project runs long.
Step 6 — Set a Timeline and Milestone Schedule

A scope of work is not just a list of tasks — it is a project management document. For each major category, specify a start date, completion date, and any dependencies (for example, electrical must be done before drywall closes up the walls). Define payment milestones tied to completion of specific work stages rather than paying large lump sums upfront. A typical structure might be 10% at contract signing, 30% at rough-in completion, 30% at drywall and paint, and the final 30% at project completion and punch list sign-off. This protects you from contractors who disappear after getting paid too much too soon.

Pro Tip: Always do a formal punch list walkthrough before making your final payment. Walk the property with your contractor and note any items that are incomplete, incorrect, or below quality standards. Put these in writing and tie the final payment to their completion. This simple step can save significant disputes and rework costs.
Common Scope of Work Mistakes to Avoid

items: Using vague language like 'update,' 'fix,' or 'repair' without specifics
Forgetting to include permit requirements for structural, electrical, or plumbing work
Skipping the contingency reserve and running out of budget mid-project
Paying too much upfront before any work is completed
Not getting the scope signed by the contractor before work begins
Leaving out material specifications, which allows contractors to use cheap substitutes
Failing to account for lead times on special-order materials like windows or cabinets

sections.content: How Your Scope of Work Connects to Your Deal Analysis

Your scope of work is not just a contractor document — it feeds directly into your deal numbers. Every line item cost rolls up into your total rehab budget, which you use to calculate your MAO, your expected profit, and your return on investment. If you are newer to real estate investing and want to understand how the full deal analysis process works before you start writing scopes of work, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners). Wholesalers assigning contracts can also benefit from understanding rehab scopes — it helps you price deals more accurately and sell them faster to experienced buyers. Our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) covers how to present rehab estimates when marketing deals to your buyer list.
